what: Hexcel makes advanced composite materials: carbon fibre, reinforcement fabrics and the resin systems that bond them into structures far lighter and stronger than aluminium. Its materials go into commercial aircraft wings and fuselages, military aircraft, helicopter rotor blades, satellites and wind turbine blades.
customers: Commercial aircraft manufacturers and their structural suppliers, defence and space programmes, and industrial customers including wind energy.
money: Carbon fibre, prepreg and reinforcement products sold by the pound into aerospace structures.
Finished composite structures and honeycomb core components.
moat: Composite materials for aircraft are qualified onto a specific aircraft programme after years of testing, and the qualification belongs to the material and the supplier together. Changing supplier means requalifying the structure, which no aircraft manufacturer will do for cost reasons. A design win therefore lasts the production life of the aircraft, which for a commercial programme is decades.
risks: The shares trade at about 34.3 times earnings and 18.0 times EV/EBITDA, which prices in a full aerospace recovery.
Revenue has flattened at about $1.9B to $2.0B, so the recovery from the pandemic trough has stalled short of growth.
A net margin of 5.8% is low for a business with this kind of qualification moat, which suggests pricing power is weaker than the lock-in implies.
Revenue depends almost entirely on commercial aircraft build rates, and both Boeing and Airbus have struggled to raise production.
Debt of $1.0B against $71.0M of cash leaves little cushion in a business this cyclical.
opportunities: Composite content per aircraft keeps rising with each new programme, because weight is the single most valuable thing to remove from an aeroplane.
Qualified positions on current aircraft programmes generate revenue for the decades those aircraft are built.
Free cash flow of $209.8M on $2.0B of revenue is solid, and the shares trade at about 27.5 times it.
Aircraft build rates are still well below the order backlog, so the volume recovery has years left in principle.
Fifteen analysts average a $98.87 target, about 30% above the current price.
watch: Aircraft build rates at Boeing and Airbus. Hexcel sells materials by the pound into aircraft structures, so production rates are not a driver of the business — they are the business.
view: Hexcel is one of the purest ways to own commercial aircraft production rates, and that is both the attraction and the problem. Its carbon fibre and prepreg are qualified onto specific aircraft programmes, which means the revenue arrives by the pound as aircraft get built. No amount of operational excellence changes that relationship: if Boeing and Airbus build more aircraft, Hexcel sells more material, and if they do not, it does not.

The qualification moat is genuine. Composite materials go through years of structural testing to be approved for an aircraft, and the approval attaches to the specific material from the specific supplier. Switching means requalifying the structure, which no airframer will do to save money on inputs. A design win therefore lasts the production life of the programme — decades for a commercial aircraft. On paper that is one of the best competitive positions in manufacturing.

What troubles me is the 5.8% net margin, because a supplier with that kind of lock-in should earn more. Compare it with ESCO’s 27% or any qualified defence component maker and the gap tells you something: Hexcel’s customers are two enormous airframers who buy by the pound and negotiate accordingly. Qualification keeps competitors out but does not confer pricing power against a monopsony. That is a crucial distinction and it caps what this business can ever earn.

At 34.3 times earnings on flat revenue, the price assumes the build-rate recovery resumes. The structural argument in favour is real — composite content per aircraft rises with each new programme because removing weight from an aeroplane is worth more than almost anything else — but it plays out over decades while the share price trades on this year’s deliveries. With $1.0 billion of debt against $71 million of cash, there is not much cushion if rates disappoint again. I would want this considerably cheaper, and I would judge it purely on Boeing and Airbus monthly deliveries, which are published and are the only input that matters.
bull: Boeing and Airbus finally raise build rates against a huge backlog while composite content per aircraft keeps rising, and operating leverage lifts a thin margin sharply.
bear: Build rates disappoint again, two powerful customers keep margins at 6%, and a 34 times multiple on flat revenue with $1 billion of debt unwinds.
